question: Best fractional CRO for a healthtech company?
body:
## Direct Answer
The best fractional CRO for a healthtech company is not a famous name but a specific profile: an operator who has personally carried a revenue number inside a regulated, clinical, or payer-facing business, who understands long enterprise sales cycles gated by compliance, and who plugs into your stage for two to three days a week without demanding equity or a full base salary. Fit beats brand every time. You are hiring a pattern of experience and a way of working, not a logo.

Healthtech is one of the hardest categories in which to hire a revenue leader, and it is precisely the category where a fractional Chief Revenue Officer earns their keep. The buying committee is large, the sales cycle is long, the regulatory surface is unforgiving, and the difference between a demo and a signed contract can be a HIPAA review, a security questionnaire, or a health system's twelve-month budget calendar. A generalist SaaS CRO who has only sold horizontal software into mid-market will drown here. Below is how to define the role, evaluate candidates, structure the engagement, and avoid the expensive mistakes that most first-time healthtech founders make.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do for a healthtech company?
A fractional CRO is a senior revenue executive who owns your entire go-to-market motion — sales, and often marketing, customer success, and revenue operations — on a part-time, fixed-fee basis. In a healthtech context, the mandate is narrower and deeper than the generic version. They are accountable for the number, but the number lives behind gates that do not exist in ordinary software: a clinical validation study, a payer contract, a health-system procurement queue, a security assessment, or an FDA pathway. The fractional CRO's first job is often not to sell but to make your revenue engine *legible* — to map who actually signs, what actually blocks, and how long each gate really takes.

In practice the engagement splits into three layers. First, diagnosis: they spend the opening thirty days inside your pipeline, your CRM, and your last twenty lost deals, producing a written picture of where revenue leaks. Second, architecture: they design the sales process, the segmentation, the compensation plan, the forecast cadence, and the tech stack that fits *your* buyer, not the buyer from their last company. Third, execution and hiring: they run the team, coach the reps, personally close the largest and most complex deals, and — critically — recruit the full-time revenue leader who will eventually replace them. A good fractional CRO is building toward their own obsolescence. That is a feature, not a bug. If you want to see how this maps to the rest of the revenue function, our guide at [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-role](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-role) breaks the responsibilities down by company stage.

The word "fractional" matters. You are not getting a consultant who writes a deck and leaves. You are getting an operator with a seat in your leadership meetings, a login to your CRM, and their name on the forecast. The fraction refers to time — typically two to three days a week — not to accountability. The best ones behave like a full-time hire who happens to also serve one or two other companies, and they bring the pattern-recognition of having seen the same problem across multiple healthtech businesses.

## Why is healthtech uniquely hard for a revenue leader?
Healthtech breaks the assumptions baked into most sales playbooks. In ordinary B2B software, the person who feels the pain is close to the person who holds the budget, and a motivated champion can pull a deal through in a quarter. In healthtech, the person who feels the pain — a nurse, a clinician, a care coordinator — is often three organizational layers away from the budget, and the budget itself may be controlled by a health system's finance office, a payer's actuarial team, or an employer's benefits committee. The champion cannot pull the deal through alone. They need air cover from compliance, security, legal, and clinical leadership, each of whom can veto but none of whom can approve.

Then there is the regulatory and trust surface. A HIPAA Business Associate Agreement is table stakes. Beyond that, buyers demand SOC 2 Type II reports, penetration test results, data-residency guarantees, and increasingly evidence of clinical efficacy or real-world outcomes. A fractional CRO who has not lived inside these gates will under-forecast the cycle, over-promise the close date, and burn credibility with the board. Reimbursement adds another dimension entirely: if your product's economics depend on a CPT code, a value-based-care arrangement, or a payer contract, your revenue leader must speak the language of medical economics fluently. This is why the healthtech CRO market is thin and why fit is everything. Our deep-dive on regulated-market sales cycles at [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/healthtech-sales-cycle](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/healthtech-sales-cycle) documents typical gate durations by buyer type.

The diagram below shows why a single champion is never enough in a healthtech deal, and why the fractional CRO's real skill is orchestrating a committee rather than charming an individual.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Clinical champion feels the pain] --> B[Builds internal case]
    B --> C[Compliance and privacy review]
    B --> D[Security assessment]
    B --> E[Clinical leadership sign off]
    C --> F[Finance and budget owner]
    D --> F
    E --> F
    F --> G[Procurement and legal]
    G --> H[Signed contract]
```

Notice that every branch must clear before the deal reaches finance, and finance sits *before* procurement, not after. Founders routinely forecast the deal as closed once the champion says yes. The fractional CRO's job is to teach the whole company that the champion's yes is the *start* of the buying process, not the end of the selling one.

## What profile should you actually hire for?
Ignore the title inflation and look for four concrete signals. First, they have personally carried and hit a revenue number inside a healthtech, medtech, digital-health, or adjacent regulated business — not merely advised one. Ask for the exact number, the exact company, and the exact years, then reference-check it. Second, they have sold into your specific buyer. "Healthtech" is not one market; selling a clinician-facing workflow tool into hospitals is a completely different motion from selling a wellness benefit into self-insured employers or a data platform into payers. A CRO who crushed it selling to providers may be useless selling to payers, and vice versa. Third, they have built, not just managed — they can show you a comp plan they designed, a sales process they documented, and a forecast model they ran. Fourth, they are comfortable being replaced; the best fractional CROs will tell you in the interview when and how they expect to hand off to a full-time hire.

Be sceptical of three profiles that look attractive and usually disappoint. The first is the big-logo enterprise seller whose entire career was inside a company with an established brand, a mature product, and inbound demand — they often cannot generate pipeline from zero. The second is the pure consultant who produces beautiful frameworks but has never lived with the consequences of a missed quarter. The third is the serial fractional who is spread across five clients and gives you the leftovers of their attention; two clients is the practical ceiling for real engagement. Our evaluation scorecard at [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-evaluation](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-evaluation) turns these signals into a weighted rubric you can run each candidate through.

Stage matters as much as sector. A seed-stage healthtech company with under a million in revenue needs a fractional CRO who will personally sell and is allergic to premature process; a Series B company at eight million in revenue needs one who will build the machine and hire the team. Hiring the machine-builder into the founder-led-sales stage produces a lot of expensive process and no revenue. Hiring the personal-closer into the scale stage produces a hero who cannot build a repeatable system. Match the operator's instinct to the phase you are actually in, not the phase you wish you were in.

## How should you structure and price the engagement?
Fractional CRO engagements are almost always priced as a fixed monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days per week, sometimes with a performance component layered on top. Do not overweight the equity conversation early; a fractional executive who demands significant equity before proving anything is usually a full-time hire in disguise who could not find a full-time seat. A modest performance bonus tied to clearly defined, mutually agreed revenue or pipeline milestones aligns incentives without turning a three-month diagnostic into an equity negotiation. Insist on a defined scope, a defined day commitment, and a thirty-day written diagnostic as the first deliverable — if they cannot commit to producing that, they are not operating, they are advising.

Structure the engagement in phases with explicit exit criteria, and put the phases in the contract. The diagram below shows a healthy arc: a short paid diagnostic, a build-and-run phase, and a deliberate handoff to a full-time leader. Each phase has a decision gate where either side can walk.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Diagnostic phase 30 days] --> B{Fit confirmed}
    B -->|Yes| C[Build and run phase]
    B -->|No| D[Clean exit]
    C --> E[Hire full time leader]
    E --> F[Structured handoff]
    F --> G[Advisory tail optional]
```

The diagnostic phase is the single most important gate and the cheapest insurance you will buy. Thirty days of a fractional CRO inside your pipeline tells you whether the chemistry works, whether their diagnosis is sharp, and whether their prescription fits your business — before you commit to a year. Treat a candidate's willingness to be evaluated on a paid diagnostic as itself a strong positive signal. Anyone confident in their operating ability will happily be judged on thirty days of real work. Our engagement-structuring template at [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-engagement](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-engagement) includes the milestone and exit-criteria language founders most often forget to negotiate.

On sourcing, the strongest channel is a warm introduction from a founder who has already used the person in a comparable healthtech business — reference-checkable, motion-specific, and pre-vetted. Fractional executive networks and specialist marketplaces are a reasonable second channel, but treat their vetting as a starting filter, not a guarantee. Your own board and investors are often the best-connected source; a healthtech-focused fund has usually watched a dozen fractional CROs succeed or fail across its portfolio and knows exactly who fits your stage and buyer.

## What are the biggest mistakes founders make when hiring one?
The most common and most expensive mistake is hiring for the number without hiring for the buyer. Founders see "CRO, hit fifty million in revenue" on a résumé and stop reading. But if that fifty million came from selling horizontal software to mid-market on a thirty-day cycle, none of the muscle transfers to a twelve-month health-system procurement gauntlet. The second mistake is treating the fractional CRO as a magic outsourced sales function and disengaging — a fractional revenue leader multiplies a founder's involvement, they do not replace it. The best outcomes come from founders who stay close, feed context, and open doors, while the CRO builds the machine.

A third mistake is skipping the reference checks that actually matter. Do not just call the references the candidate offers; back-channel to a founder or VP who reported into a deal the candidate ran, and ask the uncomfortable questions — did the forecast hold, did the reps stay, did the process survive their departure. A fourth is under-scoping the compliance and security dimension, then being blindsided when every deal stalls in a security questionnaire the CRO never mentioned. A fifth is failing to plan the handoff: the fractional CRO is temporary by design, and if you have not agreed on when and how they recruit and transition to a full-time leader, you will either lose the momentum they built or keep paying fractional rates for a role that should have gone full-time. Build the handoff into the contract on day one. Our post-mortem library at [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-mistakes](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-mistakes) catalogs these failure modes with anonymized examples from real engagements.

Finally, do not confuse activity with progress. A fractional CRO who fills your calendar with meetings, dashboards, and frameworks but does not move the number or clear the gates is expensive theater. Anchor the relationship to outcomes you defined in the diagnostic — pipeline created, gates cleared, cycle time reduced, deals closed — and review them on a fixed cadence. The whole value of the fractional model is that you can end it cleanly if the outcomes are not there. Use that leverage.

## Related questions
### How much does a fractional CRO cost?
Fractional CROs are typically priced as a monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days per week, often with a modest performance component. Costs vary widely by stage, seniority, and day commitment, so anchor on scope and outcomes rather than a single benchmark figure.

### Fractional CRO vs. VP of Sales — which does a healthtech startup need?
A VP of Sales runs a team against a defined motion; a fractional CRO designs the motion, owns the full revenue function, and often hires that VP. Early-stage healthtech usually needs the architect first, then the executor.

### When should a healthtech company hire a full-time CRO instead?
Move to full-time when the motion is proven, the pipeline is predictable, and the role needs daily presence across a growing team — usually once you have repeatable, forecastable revenue and can justify a full comp package. The fractional CRO should help you make the switch.

### Can one fractional CRO serve both sales and marketing?
Often yes at early stage, where demand generation and sales are tightly coupled and one leader can own the whole revenue funnel. As you scale, the marketing function typically splits off under its own leader while the CRO retains the number.

## FAQ
**What does the "fractional" in fractional CRO mean?**
It refers to time commitment, not accountability. A fractional CRO works part-time — commonly two to three days a week — while carrying full ownership of your revenue number, leadership-team presence, and forecast.

**How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?**
Most run six to eighteen months: a short diagnostic, a build-and-run phase, and a deliberate handoff to a full-time hire. The exact length depends on how quickly the motion becomes repeatable and a permanent leader is in place.

**Should a fractional CRO get equity?**
Sometimes a small grant is appropriate for a longer, deeply embedded engagement, but be wary of anyone demanding significant equity before proving fit. The core compensation is a fixed retainer; equity is a supplement, not the headline.

**How do I know if a fractional CRO has real healthtech experience?**
Ask for the specific company, the specific revenue number, the specific buyer type, and the years, then reference-check all four independently. Selling to providers, payers, and employers are different motions — confirm they have sold into *your* buyer.

**Can a fractional CRO help with fundraising?**
Yes. A credible revenue leader with a clean, defensible forecast and a documented go-to-market strategy strengthens your narrative with investors, and many fractional CROs join board and investor meetings to speak to the revenue plan directly.

**What is the first thing a good fractional CRO should deliver?**
A written thirty-day diagnostic: where revenue is leaking, why deals are lost, what the real sales cycle looks like, and a prescription for process, comp, and stack. If they cannot commit to producing that, they are advising, not operating.

**How is a fractional CRO different from a sales consultant?**
A consultant produces recommendations and leaves; a fractional CRO owns the number, sits in leadership meetings, runs the team, and personally closes the hardest deals. The fractional model carries operational accountability that pure consulting does not.

**Will a fractional CRO work if I only have one or two salespeople?**
Yes — in fact that is an ideal moment. At that stage the fractional CRO both sells personally and lays down the process, segmentation, and comp structure that let you hire correctly rather than expensively guessing.
